 By Ng Hui Min •

 Add us on Google The Straits Times Index (STI) declined 5.1% in October 2026, with Wilmar International, Yangzijiang Shipbuilding and Seatrium recording even sharper falls. We look at what has changed for these three Singapore blue chips, and whether their lower share prices warrant a closer look.
 In this article What happened?
 Singapore blue chip stocks fell in October.
 The Straits Times Index (STI) ended October 2026 5.1% lower, with several index constituents recording double-digit share-price declines.
 Wilmar International was the worst performer, falling 16.6%, followed by Yangzijiang Shipbuilding at 11.3% and Seatrium at 10.7%, according to FactSet.
 Interestingly, Yangzijiang Shipbuilding was the best-performing Singapore blue chip in September , before reversing course in October.
 We also previously looked at Singapore blue chip stocks trading near their 52-week lows , including Seatrium.
 With these share-price declines, I wanted to find out whether the three Singapore blue chips are worth revisiting, or whether their fundamentals suggest more caution is warranted.
 3 worst-performing Singapore blue chips in October 2026
 Rank Stock SGX code October total return 
 1 Wilmar International F34 -16.6% 
 2 Yangzijiang Shipbuilding BS6 -11.3% 
 3 Seatrium 5E2 -10.7% 
 Source: Factset  
 #1 – Wilmar International (SGX: F34): Earnings pressure and regulatory uncertainty
 Wilmar International was the worst-performing Singapore blue chip in October, with its share price falling 16.6%.
 Source: Beansprout Wilmar is one of Asia's largest agribusiness groups, with operations spanning oil palm plantations, oilseed crushing, edible oils, food products and sugar.
 Its latest third-quarter results provide some context for the weakness in its share price.
 Wilmar's 3Q26 core net profit declined despite higher revenue
 Wilmar reported revenue of US$21.66 billion for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), an increase of 13.6% year on year.
 However, core net profit fell 25.2% year on year to US$267.3 million.
 The decline reflected higher raw material costs in its food products business and weaker soybean crushing margins.
 This suggests that higher sales are not necessarily translating into stronger profitability across Wilmar's businesses.
 For investors, the more important question is whether these margin pressures are temporary or could continue into subsequent quarters.
 If raw material costs remain elevated and Wilmar is unable to pass them on to customers, its earnings could remain under pressure.
 Source: Wilmar 1H26 Results Presentation Another development in October was the disclosure of preliminary inquiries by Indonesian police into fires affecting land associated with Wilmar's subsidiaries in West Kalimantan.
 The development has added regulatory and reputational uncertainty for the company.
 How does Wilmar fare on our Fundamental Checklist?
 Wilmar passes two of the three fundamental checks.
 It passes the revenue and earnings check, with earnings per share (EPS) growth of 20.9% outpacing revenue growth of 4.5%.
 Wilmar also passes the valuation check. Its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 10.3 times and price-to-book (P/B) ratio of 0.66 times are below their historical averages, while its forward dividend yield of 5.0% is above its historical average.
 However, Wilmar is flagged on balance sheet strength, with a net debt-to-equity ratio of 129.1%, above the screener's 100% threshold.
 While Wilmar's valuation appears relatively attractive against its historical averages, its higher leverage and recent earnings pressure warrant caution.
 Source: Beansprout What to watch for Wilmar
 Wilmar's share-price decline may warrant a closer look, but the earnings outlook remains an important consideration.
 I would focus on whether its food products margins recover, whether soybean crushing profitability improves, and whether cash generation remains healthy.
 I would also monitor developments relating to the Indonesian fire inquiries.

 #2 – Yangzijiang Shipbuilding (SGX: BS6): Can strong earnings momentum continue?
 Yangzijiang Shipbuilding was the second-worst-performing Singapore blue chip in October, declining 11.3%.
 Source: Beansprout This marks a reversal from September, when Yangzijiang was the best-performing STI constituent with a total return of 6.0%.
 The company had also recorded a strong share-price rally in August, supported by robust earnings and a sizeable order book.
 The recent decline raises a question about whether expectations for its future earnings have become too optimistic.
 Yangzijiang's 1H26 earnings showed strong profitability
 Yangzijiang Shipbuilding is one of China's largest privately owned shipbuilders, producing container ships, bulk carriers and other commercial vessels.
 For the first half of 2026 (1H26), its revenue rose 36.2% year on year to 17.5 billion Chinese renminbi (RMB17.5 billion).
 Net profit attributable to shareholders increased 28.4% to RMB5.4 billion, supported by higher-priced vessel contracts and a favourable mix of ships.
 Its group gross profit margin improved to 36.2%, while its shipbuilding segment gross profit margin reached approximately 37%.
 The improvement reflects the progressive construction of vessels secured at higher contract prices, alongside a greater contribution from higher-value vessel types.
 Yangzijiang’s shipbuilding gross profit margin rose from approximately 13% in FY2022 to 37% in 1H26, reflecting higher contract prices and a more profitable mix of vessels under construction.
 Source: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding 1H26 Results Presentation A sizeable order book provides revenue visibility
 Yangzijiang reported an order book of US$22.4 billion across 256 vessels at the end of June 2026, with deliveries scheduled through 2030.
 Containerships accounted for 151 vessels in the order book, making them the largest category.
 The order book has grown significantly from US$10.5 billion at the end of 2022, although its value has remained broadly unchanged since the end of 2025.
 This provides visibility over future revenue, but does not guarantee that the group can sustain its current profit margins.
 Yangzijiang also maintained a net cash position of approximately RMB12.5 billion at the end of June 2026.
 This gives the group financial flexibility to support its operations and investment requirements.
 Source: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding 1H26 Results Presentation How does Yangzijiang fare on our Fundamental Checklist?
 Yangzijiang Shipbuilding passes two of the three checks, supported by its earnings growth and strong balance sheet.
 Its EPS growth of 30.6% exceeds revenue growth of 7.4%, allowing it to pass the revenue and earnings check.
 It also passes the balance sheet check, with a net debt-to-equity ratio of -45.3%, reflecting its net cash position.
 However, the valuation check is flagged.
 Yangzijiang's P/E ratio of 8.8 times and P/B ratio of 2.89 times are both above their historical averages, while its forward dividend yield of 4.3% is below its historical average.
 This suggests that while Yangzijiang's fundamentals remain strong, its shares may not necessarily be attractively valued relative to their own history.
 Source: Beansprout What to watch for Yangzijiang Shipbuilding
 For me, the most important question is whether Yangzijiang can continue securing new orders at attractive margins.
 Its large order book and net cash position provide financial strength, but I would also watch the pace of new orders and project execution.
 I would compare its current valuation against earnings across a full shipbuilding cycle, rather than relying solely on its recent record profitability.
 If earnings remain strong while the valuation becomes more reasonable, the recent correction could make Yangzijiang worth examining more closely.

 #3 – Seatrium (SGX: 5E2): Improving profitability, but execution risks remain
 Seatrium was the third-worst-performing Singapore blue chip in October, with its share price declining 10.7%.
 Source: Beansprout The company provides engineering solutions to the offshore, marine and energy industries, including floating production vessels, offshore wind infrastructure and ship repairs.
 Despite the share-price weakness, Seatrium's latest reported financial results showed an improvement in profitability.
 Seatrium's 1H26 underlying earnings improved
 For the first half of 2026, Seatrium reported revenue of S$5.6 billion, an increase of 4.7% year on year.
 Net profit rose to S$373 million, compared with S$144 million a year earlier.
 However, part of this increase came from divestment gains.
 Excluding these gains, net profit rose 54% to S$212 million.
 This is an important distinction because underlying earnings provide a clearer picture of how its core operations are performing.
 Seatrium's gross profit margin also improved to 8.6%, from 7.4% a year earlier.
 The improvement was supported by a better project mix, operating leverage and cost efficiencies.
 Source: Seatrium 1H26 Results Presentation How does Seatrium fare on our Fundamental Checklist?
 Seatrium is the only company among the three that passes all of our three fundamental checks.
 Its EPS growth of 105.9% exceeds revenue growth of 24.3%, meeting the revenue and earnings check.
 Seatrium also passes the balance sheet check, with a net debt-to-equity ratio of 16.6%, below the screener's 100% threshold.
 On valuation, its P/E ratio of 13.3 times and P/B ratio of 0.85 times are below their historical averages, while its forward dividend yield of 1.6% is above its historical average.
 These results suggest that Seatrium's improving fundamentals are accompanied by a valuation that compares favourably with its historical averages.
 Source: Beansprout What to watch for Seatrium
 I would focus on whether Seatrium can sustain its improvement in underlying profitability.
 Its higher gross margins and earnings growth are encouraging signs, but I would want to see continued progress in project execution and cash flow.
 I would also monitor new contract wins and whether they can support future earnings without taking on excessive execution risks.
 Source: Seatrium 1H26 Results Presentation Related links:
 Explore Seatrium's latest share price, share price target, valuation and analysis. 
 Explore Seatrium's latest dividend yield and dividend payout history 
 What would Beansprout do?
 Wilmar International, Yangzijiang Shipbuilding and Seatrium were the three worst-performing Singapore blue chips in October. 
 However, I would not assume that these stocks have become attractively valued simply because their share prices have fallen.
 For my Opportunity Pot , I would focus on three factors: whether earnings are improving, whether the balance sheet can support future growth, and whether the valuation offers sufficient potential returns for the risks involved.
 Here is how the three stocks compare across these fundamental checks.
 Stock Fundamental Checklist result What stands out Key risks 
 Wilmar International 2/3 checks Diversified agribusiness operations, earnings growth on the screener and attractive valuation relative to historical averages. High leverage, pressure on profit margins, raw material costs and regulatory uncertainty. 
 Yangzijiang Shipbuilding 2/3 checks Strong earnings growth, high ROE, net cash and large order book. Shipbuilding cycle, pace of new orders, steel costs, currencies and execution. 
 Seatrium 3/3 checks Strong underlying earnings growth, improving profit margins, manageable debt and attractive valuation relative to historical averages. Project execution, cost overruns, cash flow generation and sustainability of earnings recovery. 
 Based on our fundamental checklist, Seatrium stands out as the only company passing all three checks , although I would not treat this as a buy signal. 
 For Seatrium, I would want to see sustained underlying profitability, better cash generation and continued progress in project execution. 
 For Yangzijiang, I would focus on whether earnings can justify its valuation through the shipbuilding cycle.
 For Wilmar, I would want greater clarity on its earnings recovery, leverage and regulatory uncertainties before drawing conclusions about its valuation.
 I would therefore use the October declines as a starting point for deeper research, rather than assume that any of these stocks is due for a rebound.
